fetched_contents.text: Enhanced Monacolin K Production in Monascus purpureus Via Mutagenesis and Nitrogen Source Optimization ABSTRACT Monascus fungi are valued for their production of Monacolin K (MK), a bioactive compound with recognized lipid‐lowering and multifunctional properties. To enhance MK yield in solid‐state fermentation, this study combined atmospheric and room‐temperature plasma (ARTP) mutagenesis with L‐arginine supplementation. A mutant strain, C‐23, was obtained, and the addition of L‐arginine increased MK production by 97.3%, reaching 9.45 mg/g. Untargeted metabolomics revealed that L‐arginine reshaped metabolic pathways related to amino acids, cofactors, carbohydrates, and lipids, elucidating the mechanism behind MK overproduction. This work provides a strategic approach for developing high‐yielding Monascus strains and offers insights into the metabolic regulation of MK biosynthesis. Keywords: ARTP mutation, metabolomics, monacolin K, monascus, solid‐state fermentation ---------------------------------------- Abbreviations ARTP atmospheric and room‐temperature plasma KEGG Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes LC–MS liquid chromatography‐mass spectrometry MK monacolin K OPLS‐DA orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis PCA principal component analysis RYR red yeast rice SSF solid‐state fermentation TCA tricarboxylic acid VIP Variable Importance in Projection 1. Introduction Monascus, a widespread fungal species, has diverse and unique applications in several fields [1]. Its fermentation product, red yeast rice (RYR), has been used for thousands of years [2]. Monascus species play a key role in the food industry and many other fields, such as medicine, chemicals, and agriculture [3, 4, 5, 6]. Among their secondary metabolites, monacolin K (MK), also known as lovastatin, has become a research hotspot worldwide, owing to its lipid‐lowering and anti‐inflammatory effects. These properties of MK are attributed to its effective inhibition of 3‐hydroxy‐3‐methylglutaryl coenzyme A [7]. Recently, several methods have been developed to increase MK production by Monascus species. For example, the mutant CSUFT‐1 strain exhibited a 1.67‐fold increase in MK production during solid‐state fermentation (SSF) conditions [8]. Another Monascus strain was subjected to ultraviolet irradiation and ethyl methanesulfonate mutagenesis, resulting in varying increases in MK content [9]. Another study enhanced MK production in the mutant KU4 strain by gamma‐irradiating the spore suspension [10]. Overall, these mutagenesis methods effectively increase the content of MK produced by Monascus. In addition, MK yield can be increased by optimizing fermentation, for example, by adding amino acids and other nutrients. For example, adding glutamic acid to Monascus fermentation liquid can significantly improve MK yield [11]. Moreover, adding arginine to the Monascus fermentation broth significantly increased its MK yield from 94.6 to 228.4 mg/L [12]. The addition of soy protein isolate can also significantly alter MK metabolism [13]. The present study aimed to lay a new foundation for optimizing Monascus fermentation and increasing MK production. To this end, we used the ARTP mutation technology to obtain a Monascus mutant with increased MK yield during SSF. We also assessed the effects of adding L‐arginine to Monascus SSF on MK yield. Finally, we investigated the metabolic regulatory mechanism of L‐arginine on MK production using liquid chromatography‐mass spectrometry (LC–MS), revealing the underlying pathways responsible for enhanced MK production. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Strains Monascus M‐1 (CGMCC No. 18110) was isolated from Monascus samples collected from Monascus products in major Monascus‐producing areas in China. The sample has been deposited in the general microbiology center of the China microbiology preservation and management committee and our laboratory. The mutant strain C‐23 was mutated using the ARTP technique and is maintained in our laboratory. Rice was purchased from Heilongjiang (China). 2.2. ARTP Mutation and Screening The spore suspension was prepared by washing the spores with sterile water, then centrifuging and repeating the washes twice with sterile water. Microscopically, spore concentration was determined to be 106–108/mL. A 10 μL aliquot of the suspension was evenly spread onto the substrate, and ARTP irradiation was performed for varying durations (0, 30, 60, 75, 90, 120, 150, and 180 s). The treatment parameters were set as follows: processing distance, 2 mm; processing power, 100 W; and gas flow rate, 10 standard liters per min [14]. After processing, the sheets were placed in Eppendorf tubes containing 1 mL of an aseptic solution using aseptic tweezers. The tubes were then placed in an oscillator and allowed to oscillate for 1 min. Microorganisms attached to the slides were eluted into an aseptic solution to form a bacterial suspension. The new bacterial suspension was diluted, and 100 μL of the dilution was spread on a Petri dish. Colonies were then counted, and the lethal rate was calculated. Mutant strains were screened using SSF, and those with high MK content were selected. 2.3. MK content was determined using high‐performance liquid chromatography to analyze the genetic stability of the mutant strains [18, 19]. 2.4. fetched_contents.text: An overview of Monascus fermentation processes for monaco... 1 Introduction Monascus is a small filamentous saprophytic fungus and can be grown by inoculation into rice for fermentation, converting the rice to ‘red yeast rice’. Red yeast rice is a traditional Chinese medicine that has been used in Asian food and therapeutic applications for nearly a thousand years. Its applications include coloring, preservation of traditional foods, and treatment of indigestion, diarrhea and spleen-stomach disharmony. Monascus fermentation can produce functional substances such as pigments, monacolin K (MK) and γ-aminobutyric acid [1], but most Monascus strains can also produce citrinin that exhibits liver and kidney toxicity [2]. The presence of citrinin limits the food application of Monascus to a certain extent. MK, also known as lovastatin, was first obtained by separation from M. ruber fermentation products in 1979 by the Japanese professor Akira Endo [3]. MK inhibits cholesterol synthesis by competitively inhibiting the activity of the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMGR), thus lowering cholesterol levels in human and animal blood. The study found at least 14 substances with hypolipidemic function in red yeast rice, including MK, monacolin J, monacolin L, monacolin M, monacolin X and their acidic structures, dehydroMK, dihydromonacolin L and compactin [4]. Common fermentation modes for Monascus to produce MK include solid state fermentation (SSF) and submerged fermentation (SmF). In fermentation optimization studies for MK production by Monascus, most research has focused on SSF methods because they offer has many advantages compared to SmF methods. Fungi can produce more enzymes and secondary metabolites in SSF, and some enzymes can only be produced in SSF [5]. Zhang et al. [6, 7] utilized SSF by adding agar to a liquid medium, then inoculating Monascus into the solid medium cut into small pieces, and used a liquid medium without agar for fermentation comparison. Compared with Monascus SmF, biomass accumulation, MK synthesis rate, glycerol consumption rate, cell membrane fluidity and permeability, and glycerol tolerance concentration in Monascus under SSF conditions were significantly higher. Furthermore, MK yield of Monascus under SSF is usually several to dozens of times higher than that under SmF [8, 9]. Scholars have previously reviewed the research progress in lovastatin production by Aspergillus terreus fermentation [10]. Herein, we comprehensively review the research progress in MK production using Monascus fermentation processes, from the breeding of high-yield MK strains to the optimization of fermentation medium and fermentation conditions, including SSF and SmF methods. 2 Monascus strain breeding for high-yield MK production Monascus strain choice has an important influence on production of MK by fermentation, and the ability of different strains to produce MK under the same culture conditions varies greatly. Usually, mutagenesis of Monascus is performed using separation and screening [11, 12, 13] or by physical or chemical methods to obtain strains with high yield of MK, thereby significantly increasing MK yield and reducing citrinin content. Suh et al. [14] obtained multiple mutants with high MK yields through γ-ray treatment, among which the KU609 mutant had the highest MK yield, nearly 10 times higher than the original strain. After optimization of culture conditions, MK yield of KU609 can reach 977 mg/kg. There are also studies on mutagenesis of Monascus strains by combining ultraviolet (UV) irradiation and LiCl treatment. UV irradiation for 45s was performed under 1.0% LiCl conditions, then five mutant strains were obtained after three rounds of irradiation. M. purpureus ZT35, a strain with high MK yield, was obtained through five generations of culture, which has a MK yield that is three times higher than that of the original strain [15]. In addition, MK synthesis by Monascus has a competitive relationship with the synthesis of red pigment. Studies have shown that treatment of Monascus spores with UV irradiation or ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) can result in an albino strain that does not produce red pigment and citrinin, and its MK yield is significantly higher than that of the original strain [16]. 3 Optimization of fermentation medium for MK production by Monascus Due to the two fermentation modes of Monascus, SSF and SmF, and the significant difference in the composition of medium between SSF and SMF [5], this paper reviews the optimization of SSF and SMF medium components respectively. 3.1 Optimization of solid medium components The types of substrates and nutrient additives were optimized to increase the MK production by Monascus SSF (see Table 1 for details). fetched_contents.text: An overview of Monascus fermentation processes for monaco... 1 Introduction Monascus is a small filamentous saprophytic fungus and can be grown by inoculation into rice for fermentation, converting the rice to ‘red yeast rice’. Red yeast rice is a traditional Chinese medicine that has been used in Asian food and therapeutic applications for nearly a thousand years. Its applications include coloring, preservation of traditional foods, and treatment of indigestion, diarrhea and spleen-stomach disharmony. Monascus fermentation can produce functional substances such as pigments, monacolin K (MK) and γ-aminobutyric acid [1], but most Monascus strains can also produce citrinin that exhibits liver and kidney toxicity [2]. The presence of citrinin limits the food application of Monascus to a certain extent. MK, also known as lovastatin, was first obtained by separation from M. ruber fermentation products in 1979 by the Japanese professor Akira Endo [3]. MK inhibits cholesterol synthesis by competitively inhibiting the activity of the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMGR), thus lowering cholesterol levels in human and animal blood. The study found at least 14 substances with hypolipidemic function in red yeast rice, including MK, monacolin J, monacolin L, monacolin M, monacolin X and their acidic structures, dehydroMK, dihydromonacolin L and compactin [4]. Common fermentation modes for Monascus to produce MK include solid state fermentation (SSF) and submerged fermentation (SmF). In fermentation optimization studies for MK production by Monascus, most research has focused on SSF methods because they offer has many advantages compared to SmF methods. Fungi can produce more enzymes and secondary metabolites in SSF, and some enzymes can only be produced in SSF [5]. Zhang et al. [6, 7] utilized SSF by adding agar to a liquid medium, then inoculating Monascus into the solid medium cut into small pieces, and used a liquid medium without agar for fermentation comparison. Compared with Monascus SmF, biomass accumulation, MK synthesis rate, glycerol consumption rate, cell membrane fluidity and permeability, and glycerol tolerance concentration in Monascus under SSF conditions were significantly higher. Furthermore, MK yield of Monascus under SSF is usually several to dozens of times higher than that under SmF [8, 9]. Scholars have previously reviewed the research progress in lovastatin production by Aspergillus terreus fermentation [10]. Herein, we comprehensively review the research progress in MK production using Monascus fermentation processes, from the breeding of high-yield MK strains to the optimization of fermentation medium and fermentation conditions, including SSF and SmF methods. 2 Monascus strain breeding for high-yield MK production Monascus strain choice has an important influence on production of MK by fermentation, and the ability of different strains to produce MK under the same culture conditions varies greatly. Usually, mutagenesis of Monascus is performed using separation and screening [11, 12, 13] or by physical or chemical methods to obtain strains with high yield of MK, thereby significantly increasing MK yield and reducing citrinin content. Suh et al. [14] obtained multiple mutants with high MK yields through γ-ray treatment, among which the KU609 mutant had the highest MK yield, nearly 10 times higher than the original strain. After optimization of culture conditions, MK yield of KU609 can reach 977 mg/kg. There are also studies on mutagenesis of Monascus strains by combining ultraviolet (UV) irradiation and LiCl treatment. UV irradiation for 45s was performed under 1.0% LiCl conditions, then five mutant strains were obtained after three rounds of irradiation. M. purpureus ZT35, a strain with high MK yield, was obtained through five generations of culture, which has a MK yield that is three times higher than that of the original strain [15]. In addition, MK synthesis by Monascus has a competitive relationship with the synthesis of red pigment. Studies have shown that treatment of Monascus spores with UV irradiation or ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) can result in an albino strain that does not produce red pigment and citrinin, and its MK yield is significantly higher than that of the original strain [16]. 3 Optimization of fermentation medium for MK production by Monascus Due to the two fermentation modes of Monascus, SSF and SmF, and the significant difference in the composition of medium between SSF and SMF [5], this paper reviews the optimization of SSF and SMF medium components respectively. 3.1 Optimization of solid medium components The types of substrates and nutrient additives were optimized to increase the MK production by Monascus SSF (see Table 1 for details). fetched_contents.text: Effect of water activity, temperature, and incubation period on fungal growth and ochratoxin A production on Nyjer seeds Mycotoxin Res. 2019 Feb;35(1):1-8. doi: 10.1007/s12550-018-0325-2. Epub 2018 Aug 13. Authors Affiliations * 1 Department of Chemistry and Physics, Purdue University Northwest, Hammond, IN, 46323, USA. dgizache@pnw.edu. * 2 Department of Biological Sciences, Purdue University Northwest, Hammond, IN, 46323, USA. * 3 , Schererville, IN, 46375, USA. * PMID: 30105736 * DOI: 10.1007/s12550-018-0325-2 Abstract Aspergillus fresenii and Aspergillus sulphureus produce ochratoxin A (OTA), which is a secondary metabolite of Aspergillus and Penicillium species, with nephrotoxic effects and potential carcinogenic activity. The aim of this study was to determine the effects of temperature (20, 30, and 37 °C), water activity (0.82, 0.86, 0.90, 0.94, and 0.98 aw), incubation period (5, 10, 15, and 30 days) on fungal growth, and OTA production by A. fresenii and A. sulphureus on Nyjer oil seeds. There was no fungal growth at 0.82 aw. The two fungal species were able to produce OTA from the fifth day of incubation from 0.86 to 0.98 aw and temperature 20 to 37 °C. Aspergillus fresenii produced the highest concentration of OTA (643 μg/kg) at 0.90 aw and 37 °C within 15 days, while A. sulphureus produced the highest level of OTA (724 μg/kg) at 0.98 aw and 20 °C within 10 days. The optimum water activity and temperature for the growth of both fungi were similar at 0.94 aw and at 30 °C. There was statistically significant difference between the levels of OTA production among the two fungi. Overall, A. sulphureus produced significantly higher levels of OTA (p < 0.05). Higher temperature (37 °C) and 0.90-0.94 aw were optimal for OTA production by A. fresenii. Our results show that Nyjer seeds can support the growth of A. fresenii and A. sulphureus and OTA production, and the two species had similar temperature and water activity requirements for growth but different requirements for OTA production on Nyjer seeds. Evidence base for moisture content affecting Monascus fermentation

The evidence base is strongest for moisture content effects on secondary metabolite production, particularly MK yield, but thinner for direct pigment-specific moisture studies. Across the provided material, moisture content appears to be a process-variable constraint rather than a central focus of the cited studies, and the most direct moisture-fermentation link is the stated moisture range in a review of Monascus fermentation processes. The review explicitly states that “water content between 60%-70% can be optimal for the MK yield and biomass of the filamentous fungus,” and that this may be due to the presence of certain factors affecting the process [N1-R3]. A later fetch excerpt from the same overview also reports that under conditions of 72.5% initial water content and 38 days of fermentation time, MK yield could reach up to 6428 mg/kg [N3-F3]. This suggests that moisture content is operationally important for MK production, but the cited material does not provide a full mechanistic explanation of why this range is optimal in every case.

For pigment production, the evidence is more indirect. The overview notes that Monascus fermentation produces pigments, monacolin K, and γ-aminobutyric acid, while also noting that most strains can produce citrinin, which is toxic [N3-F3]. Another excerpt from the same overview states that Monascus fermentation can produce at least 14 hypolipidemic substances, including MK, monacolin J, monacolin L, monacolin M, monacolin X and their acidic structures, dehydroMK, dihydromonacolin L and compactin [N3-F3]. A separate search result mentions that substrates with soaking affect mold growth and secondary metabolites production, and that starch and moisture contents of substrates affect mold growth and those secondary metabolites production [N1-R4]. However, none of the provided evidence explicitly ties a specific moisture level to pigment yield or pigment composition in a published Monascus study. The closest direct evidence is the general statement that moisture content and soaking affect secondary metabolite production, but this is phrased in a way that covers both pigments and monacolin K broadly rather than isolating pigment-only effects [N1-R4].

On reported moisture ranges and corresponding fermentation outcomes, the evidence base is uneven. The clearest moisture range is 60–70% for MK yield and biomass [N1-R3], while a specific fermentation case reports 72.5% initial water content and 38 days of fermentation time [N3-F3]. Another search result mentions that substrates with soaking affect mold growth and secondary metabolites production, but the moisture range is not quantified in the excerpt [N1-R4]. The evidence therefore supports a range of 60–70% as a likely optimal or near-optimal moisture window, but it does not yet establish a universally consistent moisture threshold across all studies.

Regarding how moisture interacts with other process variables, the evidence is suggestive rather than fully quantitative. The overview notes that culture temperature is critical for growth and secondary metabolite production [N6-R4]. A separate fermentation overview states that optimization variables such as moisture content, pH, temperature, and aeration can be strategically modulated [N6-R2]. The water activity study on Nyjer seeds shows that temperature and water activity jointly affect fungal growth and mycotoxin production, with temperature 20–37 °C and water activity 0.82–0.98 aw being tested, and that higher temperature and 0.90–0.94 aw were optimal for OTA production by one species [N5-F4]. This is not Monascus-specific, but it is relevant because it shows that moisture-related parameters such as water activity and temperature can interact to shape metabolite outcomes. The fermentation overview also mentions that moisture content can be optimized through pretreatment to promote microbial fermentation [N6-R5], indicating an interaction between moisture management and process optimization.

Overall, the evidence base for moisture content affecting Monascus fermentation is strongest for MK yield and weakest for direct pigment studies. The most defensible conclusions are that moisture content can be a key factor in optimizing MK yield and biomass, that a broad moisture range of around 60–70% appears relevant, and that moisture interacts with temperature and aeration through broader fermentation optimization principles, though the exact interaction details are not fully resolved in the provided evidence [N1-R3][N3-F3][N6-R2][N6-R4][N5-F4].

How substrate moisture affects microbial physiology and metabolite synthesis

Substrate moisture affects microbial physiology and metabolite synthesis through multiple interacting mechanisms, and the evidence base here is broad but not fully mechanistic. First, moisture content is central to water activity, which directly shapes microbial viability and metabolic activity. The overview notes that culture temperature is critical for growth and secondary metabolite production, and that fermentation optimization variables such as moisture content, pH, temperature, and aeration can be strategically modulated [N6-R4][N6-R2]. A separate water activity study on fungal growth and OTA production shows that temperature and water activity jointly affect growth and mycotoxin production, with the optimal combination depending on the species and metabolite [N5-F4]. This indicates that moisture-related parameters such as water activity are not simply passive environmental variables but active regulators of microbial physiology and secondary metabolite pathways.

Second, moisture influences nutrient availability and oxygen transfer. The overview states that Monascus fermentation is performed on moist solid material in SSF, and that substrates can be optimized with different nutrient additives to increase MK production [N2-R1][N3-F3]. The review on solid-state fermentation notes that moisture-drive microbiota is a critical contributor to flavor formation and provides the theoretical basis for moisture control [N2-R2]. This implies that moisture affects how nutrients are available to the microorganisms, likely through interactions with substrate structure and diffusion. The evidence also suggests that oxygen transfer is part of the optimization picture, because SSF and SmF differ in their fermentation modes and that fermentation conditions can be adjusted [N6-R2]. Although the provided evidence does not directly quantify oxygen transfer under different moisture levels, it does support the general principle that moisture affects oxygen supply and microbial physiology.

Third, moisture relates to enzyme activity and secondary metabolite pathways. The overview states that fungi can produce more enzymes and secondary metabolites in SSF, and that some enzymes can only be produced in SSF [N3-F3]. It also notes that fermentation optimization studies for MK production have focused on SSF because of these advantages [N3-F3]. The water activity study on Nyjer seeds further shows that changes in water activity and temperature alter metabolite production, and that these conditions can shift fungal behavior from growth to toxin production [N5-F4]. While the Monascus-specific evidence does not provide a detailed molecular pathway for moisture-mediated enzyme activation, it does support the broader principle that moisture influences microbial metabolism and pathway outcomes. The fermentation overview also states that optimization variables such as moisture content, pH, temperature, and aeration can be strategically modulated, which suggests that moisture is part of a wider regulatory network controlling secondary metabolite synthesis [N6-R2].

In sum, substrate moisture affects microbial physiology and metabolite synthesis by shaping water activity, nutrient availability, and oxygen transfer, and by influencing enzyme activity and secondary metabolite pathways. The evidence supports a mechanistic model in which moisture is not merely a passive physical condition but an active determinant of microbial viability and metabolite output, though the exact pathway-level details for Monascus are not fully specified in the provided material [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-F3][N5-F4][N6-R2].

How temperature and aeration modulate pigment and monacolin K production

Temperature and aeration are both important modulators of pigment and monacolin K production, according to the provided evidence, but the evidence is uneven in detail. Temperature primarily affects microbial growth and metabolite yield by altering the physiological state of the fungus and the conditions under which secondary metabolites are synthesized. The overview notes that culture temperature is critical for the growth of filamentous fungi and the production of secondary metabolites [N6-R4]. The water activity study on Nyjer seeds shows that temperature and water activity jointly affect fungal growth and mycotoxin production, with the two fungal species tested showing different optimal combinations: A. fresenii produced the highest OTA at 0.90 aw and 37 °C, while A. sulphureus produced the highest OTA at 0.98 aw and 20 °C [N5-F4]. This is not Monascus-specific, but it is directly relevant because it shows how temperature interacts with moisture-related parameters to shape metabolite outcomes.

Aeration affects oxygen supply and secondary metabolite pathways. The review on solid-state fermentation notes that fermentation optimization variables such as moisture content, pH, temperature, and aeration can be strategically modulated [N6-R2]. The water activity study also states that culture conditions such as temperature, aeration, pH of the medium, incubation time, and composition of medium can affect the production of desired metabolites [N5-R5]. Although the provided evidence does not give a Monascus-specific aeration protocol, it does establish a general principle that aeration is an important fermentation variable affecting secondary metabolism. In SSF, oxygen transfer is especially relevant because the process operates on moist solid material without free-flowing liquid, and moisture management is linked to microbial fermentation [N2-R1][N6-R5]. This suggests that aeration can influence whether the fungus favors growth, primary metabolism, or secondary metabolite production.

Temperature × aeration interactions can change product profiles, but the evidence here is indirect rather than fully quantified. The water activity study shows that temperature and water activity together determine metabolite outcomes, and that different species may respond differently under the same conditions [N5-F4]. This implies that temperature and aeration-like parameters can act synergistically or antagonistically depending on the organism and the metabolite being produced. The fermentation overview also states that moisture content, pH, temperature, and aeration can be strategically modulated, reinforcing that these variables are not independent controls but part of a coordinated optimization framework [N6-R2]. The review on solid-state fermentation adds that moisture-drive microbiota is a critical contributor to flavor formation and that moisture control provides the theoretical basis for optimization [N2-R2], which is consistent with the idea that temperature and aeration can jointly shape product profiles.

For pigment and monacolin K specifically, the evidence is more limited. The overview states that Monascus fermentation produces pigments, monacolin K, and γ-aminobutyric acid, and that some strains also produce citrinin [N3-F3]. It also notes that MK yield can be optimized by SSF and that temperature is critical for secondary metabolite production [N6-R4]. However, the provided material does not provide a direct temperature × aeration study on pigment or MK in Monascus, so the conclusions must be general rather than Monascus-specific. The water activity study on OTA production supports the broader principle that temperature and aeration-like conditions can alter metabolite profiles, while the fermentation overview supports the idea that these variables can be modulated to optimize fermentation outcomes [N5-F4][N6-R2].

Overall, the evidence suggests that temperature modulates microbial growth and metabolite yield by altering physiological state and secondary metabolite pathways, and that aeration affects oxygen supply and secondary metabolism. The interaction between temperature and aeration can change product profiles, but the provided evidence does not establish the exact shape of that interaction for pigment and monacolin K in Monascus [N5-F4][N6-R2][N6-R4].

Optimal moisture conditions for pigment and monacolin K production

The evidence suggests that optimal moisture conditions for Monascus fermentation are not a single universal value but a moisture window that depends on the process goal and fermentation context. The clearest moisture range directly reported in the literature is 60–70% water content, which is described as optimal for MK yield and biomass of the filamentous fungus [N1-R3]. A specific fermentation case reports 72.5% initial water content and 38 days of fermentation time, yielding MK up to 6428 mg/kg [N3-F3]. These findings indicate that moisture content is operationally important for maximizing MK production, but they do not yet establish a single moisture level that optimizes both pigment and MK equally.

For pigment production, the evidence is less direct. The overview states that Monascus fermentation produces pigments, monacolin K, and γ-aminobutyric acid, but it does not provide a moisture-specific pigment yield [N3-F3]. Another excerpt notes that substrates with soaking affect mold growth and secondary metabolites production, and that starch and moisture contents affect those secondary metabolites [N1-R4]. However, the provided evidence does not separate pigment-specific effects from broader secondary metabolite effects, so the optimal moisture for pigment production cannot be determined from the cited material with confidence. The best-supported conclusion is that moisture is relevant for secondary metabolite production in general, but pigment-specific optimization remains thin in the provided evidence [N1-R4][N3-F3].

Tradeoffs between pigment yield, monacolin K yield, and fermentation efficiency are also evident. The overview notes that MK production can be optimized by SSF and that temperature is critical for secondary metabolite production [N3-F3][N6-R4]. It also states that MK yield can be several to dozens of times higher under SSF than under SmF [N3-F3]. This implies that fermentation efficiency is often linked to secondary metabolite yield rather than pigment yield. The evidence does not directly compare pigment-to-MK ratios across moisture levels, but it does suggest that optimization is a tradeoff between process conditions, secondary metabolite types, and fermentation time [N3-F3][N6-R2]. A likely interpretation is that lower moisture may favor biomass or some metabolites, while higher moisture may favor MK yield, but the exact tradeoff depends on strain, substrate, and other process variables [N1-R3][N3-F3].

Conditions under which one product dominates over the other are not explicitly quantified in the provided evidence, but the literature background supports the idea that product dominance is process-variable dependent. The overview notes that MK synthesis by Monascus has a competitive relationship with the synthesis of red pigment [N3-F3]. This indicates that the same strain may favor one product over the other depending on environmental conditions. The fermentation overview also emphasizes that optimization variables such as moisture content, pH, temperature, and aeration can be strategically modulated [N6-R2]. Together, these findings suggest that one product can dominate when the process is optimized for that outcome, but the provided evidence does not specify the exact moisture or other conditions under which pigment or monacolin K dominates [N3-F3][N6-R2].

Overall, the evidence base points to a moisture window of around 60–70% as a likely optimal range for maximizing MK yield and biomass, while pigment production remains less directly quantified. The tradeoffs suggest that higher MK yield may come at the expense of pigment yield or fermentation efficiency, and that product dominance is likely determined by the interaction of moisture with other process variables rather than moisture alone [N1-R3][N3-F3][N6-R2][N6-R4].

## Summary of the evidence

The available evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: moisture content is a central operational variable in Monascus-fermented rice solid-state fermentation, but it does not act as a single universal optimizer for pigment and monacolin K production.
